blocks.x:
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
JOE THOMAS (W. Stanley Dance) - Tape 1
Well, where were you born, Joe?
Well, Stanley, I was born in Webster Groves, Missouri.
And when?
Well, now that's (quite) a decision there. I first reported born July 24th, 1912 but after looking into a few things I find it to be July 24th, 1909.
Well, now which do you think is right?
I go for '09.
You do?
Yes.
You think that's true?
Yeah.
Well, you're older than I am.

And, the thing about it that's really important is in body Missouri I found out that they have no records of any born before 1910 but looking in the family Bible, you know, I found out it was July 24th, 1909.
They wouldn't have made a mistake in there.
I doubt it.
Well, were your parents musical at all?
Well, Stan, I thought so. My mother sang in the choir. She had not a trained voice but a very plaintive voice and I had it had something to say
J. Thomas
a chance to play in that choir some years ago as a boy.
What did you play?
The spirituals.
Yeah but what instrument?
The trumpet.
Well, how did you get to play trumpet. I mean how did that come about?
Well, that came about through ... respect for kids have to have something to do and he thought the ideas of Mr. Harvey J. Sims.
Is that two m's in Sims?

No, one m. And, he'd gone to Lincoln University in course, it's Jeff City, which is Jefferson City, you know, but we call it Jeff City. And he came back with this idea of giving the kids something to do. And he was sort of a crippled fellow. Something happened with one leg but he was very active, very thoughtful and he decided to get a bunch of kids together and to form a little band.
Was this in connection with the church or not?
I'm glad you asked that No. In fact it wasn't.
How big a place was Webster Groves?
Oh, 10,000-15,000, something like that. I'm glad you the asked that question because they gave it the name of/Douglas Band Boys but it wasn't - that was the name of the school we
J THOMAS (1) 3
but it wasn't went to, the grammar school - in connection with the school Because either. The school gave us nothing but a place to rehearse. Our families bought the uniforms and the instruments.

I haven't had a chance to talk about my dad. Now he, about the musical ideas, he was a deacon of the church and sometimes on a Sunday afternoon after the collection was passed, the deacon starts the song off, you know -- I once was blind but now I see, was dead but now I live (singing) -- and it got to be the thing that went through the whole church. So, I thought they both were musical.
He had a good voice, did he?
Well, he had a voice, a pleasing voice and he seemed to get to the people which is important.

Now, you want me to talk to you about Mr. Sims. His idea to get the kids together, keep them out of trouble, you know. I don't know what kind of trouble we could have gotten into in Webster Groves because that's a long time ago, you know. ...
(both talking)
So, he got this band together. I think I must have been, Stan, well, around 8 years old and he found a very fine teacher. I always think he's one of the finest, Mr. P. B. Langford.
Oh, yeah.
JT THOMAS (1) 4
Yeah, tremendous, out of St. Louis, tremendous teacher.
How far from St. Louis was Webster Groves?
I would think about 12 miles.
Well, that was really quite handy.
Well, handy for the kids because we could take a little car ride and get into town.
How do you spell Langford?
D: This has it L-dnk...
L-a-n-g-f-o-r-d. And a tremendous man. The man knew, the teacher knew how to handle kids. The word they use now is relate. Well, he could relate to kids. And the kids loved him.
What did he do, was that his living? Was he a teacher by profession?

Well, he was a teacher by profession, a professional allowed musician. A tremendous musician and he allowed us a certain amount of leniency. There was, I mean there's baseball and all those things and he was patient enough, he called the time but he was patient enough to give you a break of 5 or 10 minutes sun is before it happened. You know, sunshine shining, too. And he was a tremendous teacher. He has written some things, Sousa had honored him by doing one of his marches and I can't remember just what one of the marches it was. Tremendous musician.
Do you know where he was educated at all?
JTHOMAS (1)
No, I don't.
Because he must have had, he must have been a well-schooled musician originally.

Tremendous. He played everything. He's a tremendous musician. He played the trumpet, the cornet rather but he could instruct the trombone, the clarinet, the drums. Yes, he's a tremendous musician and a tremendous person. And he could impart what he wanted to impart to you.
Which is something else. Without
Without making you feel dumb, you know.
Yeah.
Which we were. Yeah, we were
So, your first instrument was trumpet?
Oh, yes. Cornet.
And he taught you from the beginning?

Well, he started us off and the difference from a kid learning an instrument like a cornet or trumpet, I found it is the balance. It's hard for a kid with small hands to balance the trumpet where a cornet is easier to balance and it makes him feel closer to the instrument.
You mean because of the length of the arms?
JTTHOMAS (1)

The length of the arms of the kids and the kids, naturally, their little arms would tip down. He can't hold it. He could get a complex from that. But with the cornet, he can hold it at least in his arms and then he get another complex.
What do you mean?
He still got to blow it.
Well, was that your choice of instruments? Was that what you wanted to play?
I don't know. I really don't know. I don't know whether it was or not.
So many kids, so many musicians who play trombone trombone were obviously attracted by the look of the . You know the guy out front sliding and everything.
No, I don't know. You see, around that time I was a pretty active kid so I don't know if it was my choice or not. I really couldn't definitely say about that whether it was or not.
Because who bought the instrument?

Our families bought the instruments. The school, the board of education had nothing to do with it. They gave us a place to rehearse and our families bought the instruments, uniforms, paid for our lessons. But, we were very fortunate in that somebody thought about us.
Did you like it right away?
I loved it.
JTHOMAS (1)
You did?
Yeah. I loved it tremendously. It gave me -- let me see what I might say, Stan -- a sense of doing something. And that first cornet, you should have seen it.
Was it an old one?
Oh, it was battered and beaten around but to me, it was the prettiest thing on earth, you know. So, I got me some -- I think it cost $7, which my parents paid for.
Which was quite a lot of money then.
For them, you know.
Yeah, but those days, I mean, that would be worth $50 now.

I guess it would be really. So, I got this old cornet and in fact they got it for me and I got me some BonAmi. And it was all black where it had been tarnished, you know, and the valves wouldn't work. So, Mr. Langford had told us about the use of kerosene to clean the pistons and all those things to run it through, you know. And, of course, Ivory soap to run it through. And I shined that horn and I shined that horn and we had a little wood shed in the backyard and I used to go out there to do my wood shedding and it was a tremendous experience because I found out I was doing something. And getting back to the teacher, he gave us a bit of theory so we had something to do and it got to be nip and tuck between the trumpet and baseball. Really and truly.
JTHOMAS (1) 8
How many kids would be in this band?
Roughly I'd say from 15 to 25.
So you were like a marching band, were you?

Oh, yes, it was a marching band and, yes, definitely it was a marching band. Marching bands have a certain amount of cadence you have to keep which also keeps a kid in line. He doesn't know, you know, about cadence and trying to do the things that should be done along with someone else.
Well, that was very good training right away.

Tremendous experience. In fact that was when I was through 8 years old. I stayed with Mr. Langford school through grammar sheeel. Webster Groves, that's my home town, and it had gotten to a point, I think we were one of the first bands to have, they have a thing they used to do called Armistice Day and after I got to be able to do a few things there, he'd make you march down to a point on Lockwood Avenue on November 11th, I think it was. And he called on me one day to play Taps but it was cold, you know. Cold as the dickens out there, you know, and so they say you put up a trumpet to your chops and it's cold, you can pull the skin off. At least I'd learned that, you know. So nobody told me and so they said we want you to play "Taps." I said, "Me?" It was an honor. I was scared first if I could play it. But that was a thing that happened yearly until I got out of ...
JTHOMAS (1)
Oh, you always used to play it?
Oh, yeah.
Well, then in other words, you were kind of star pupil in that band?
I don't know if I was the star pupil or not.
Well, I mean I take it there were several trumpet players.
Oh, yeah. We had four or five trumpet players.
Well, they're not going to ask the worst ones.
I thought they were kidding me.
Well, I mean you weren't particularly small or anything, were you?
No, I was a pretty good sized boy.
You must have been the best trumpet player.
Well, I wouldn't say that.
But you would imagine so. Did P. G. Langford come out to Webster Groves each week?

Each week. We lived across from the school. That's where our home is now, my brother's home and each week he'd come out to Webster Groves and give us our instruction. Now we first went to Mr. Sims' home where we first got together and the selection of this thing was a gasser. He said, 'Well, what do you think you want to play, young fellow?' One of the guys said, 'Well, I think I want to play the thing that slides.' Another guy said, 'Well,
J THOMAS (1) 10

I think I want to play what is that black thing with the keys on it, the clarinet." He says to me, "Well, what do you want to play?" So I guess I looked pretty husky to him for a kid. He said, "Well, you're the cornet player."
Oh, that's how you come to be--you didn't really have a preference.

Not really. The idea of Mr. Sims, as I've seen it helpful later, and Mr. Langford together and they were selfer, not forceful. You had a choice which does make a difference. We had a choice to do these things and it came out pretty good. We had to go to swimming earlier. Band rehearsal would come around 1 o'clock in the day and that was our swimming time, the time we'd go swimming. It was hot out there in the summertime in Webster Groves, Missouri. So then we'd have to go swimming earlier because we had to make a choice because we had to get to band reahearsal. We wanted to get to band rehearsal.
Of course, the uniforms were a big thing with kids, always weren't they?
I disliked them.
But a lot of kids always used to like
Yeah, kids used to like uniforms, but I dislike uniforms.
Oh, the uniform, the first time I had one, you know, I thought tremendous it was the most tremendous thing I'd ever seen in my life.
We had the band caps, up on the top was DBB and you know the band uniforms and there's a little gold there, a little silver there. And there was that certain idea it would give you.
JTHOMAS (1) 11

So sometimes we'd parade with the bands in St. Louis and there were quite a few tremendous bands at that time--Oddfellows Band, Masonic Band, oh, the A, D and D of Id (?) Band-- so it was a tremendous thing. And they had the kids bands. So, being the country boys, they invited us since Mr. Langford naturally was in that circle of musicians.

But, there was one day I'll never forget. They had those blocks in the street with I think it was asphalt they had on them. That day it must have been, I don't know, it seemed like 190 degrees and we were walking down the street and you got your drum major in front and as you turned the corner you step. And as you stepped, I stepped in asphalt, off comes my shoe but keep on marching.
You mean it was sticky?
Ohm yes. It was hot. It melted.
Just like stepping into mud.

Right. But, only it was hotter. So, the guy in back of me picked up my shoe and we kept on marching. And that, to me, Stanley, had a tremendous influence on my life this way that the people thought enough of us to get us together. And I think out of Webster Groves, Missouri, we possible had the first school band out there. I might be a liar for that but I think we had the first school band in Webster Groves, Mo., which was not sponsored by the school, which was sponsored by our parents. That's a tremendous thing, too.
JTHOMAS (1) 12
WD: very (?)

And it was a nice thing. I was there from 8 to 12. I finished grammar school at 12 and my instruction I thought was tremendous. I had a chance to appreciate that later on but the funny part about it is, now you spoke about $7 being a lot of money so one thing the parents wanted to know was how do you know this boy will get to play the trumpet $7, you know. Seven dollars is $7. So they had to (schedule) it as my mother and father always did. She said, 'Well, give him a chance.' And after they saw my interest, you know, they (paid) it.
Well, from their point of view, it was a darn good investment because it gave you something to interest you, didn't it? as you grew up?
It did, it really and truly did.
What did you do after you left grammar school?
Oh, after grammar school I went to the Lincoln University and high school in Jeff City.
Oh, Jefferson City?
Yes. Well, Lincoln University is Jeff City. The proper name, of course, is Jefferson City, Missouri.
How far away is that from ...
In 125 miles. May I talk about that for a minute?
Sure. Talk about whatever you want to talk about.
And the preparation for the trip? So, when something happened I think it was in the course of a football game that I'd gone to see. Now in Missouri, in Webster Groves,
JTHOMAS (1)

you were allowed to go to high school at that particular time without any choice. We couldn't go to the high schools in Webster Groves because they had a segregated policy there which, of course, was very stupid but that was the policy.
At the time of...
Yeah, you know. And it's time for it/stop really.
Yeah but it was a time when it still existed.

It still existed and we were victims of it so I didn't want to go to Sumner. And a little incident happened at the football game and I didn't like the sportsmanship, my idea of good teams. So, something happened to the sportsmanship I didn't like, I said, "I don't want to go to that school." So I had to explain because the difference in going to Sumner and to Lincoln is tuition and books and you know all that sort of thing.
How far away would Sumner be?
St. Louis was only 12 miles.
Oh, I see so which would have been much handier.

Much handier but something about the school that I didn't, the curriculum was tremendous. But I guess I was, what you might say, sports oriented and all that sort of thing. So we sat down and talked about it. I must tell you this, Stan, I had tremendous parents.
Were there any other children?
Yes.
How many?
JTHOMAS (1) 14
Two brothers and a sister.
I see so they had four of you.
At that time there were three of us. My sister came later. And, of course, we wanted to send her back but we couldn't.
Where did you come in the family? Are you the oldest?

I'm the oldest, yes.
So, now to get back to Lincoln. On the way to Lincoln ...
Well, now how did they arrange for you to go there?

Damn if I know. It was money, of course. It was money they couldn't afford and I guess they had gone to see Mr. Sims to get registration and all those things together but the state had nothing to do with it. You know, the State of Missouri had nothing to do with it, I mean, so far as footing the bill of expenses. You go, I mean we say you go or you pay. You know that's the score there. So, in going to, they gave me the go sign. Well, fortunately during that summer I don't know if you've ever seen short pants.
Gee, I can't remember them.
You're an Englishman, you might call them knickers.
Oh, yeah, thats right. They wore them here?
Yeah.
They never wore them in England much.
I had to wear them, man.
Because I remember a cousin of mine coming from Canada and we thought that was the funniest thing we'd ever seen.
JTHOMAS (1) 15
Of course, they used to wear them in England but they'd gone out.

Well, what happened, too, I think, in fact I know now, you don't want a kid to grow up too fast. Let him grow up with respect, you know, which I don't think that had anything to with it, the short pants, but that was their thought.
Now, where are we now?
Well, you're going off to Lincoln? But, you've got to board there. Who were you going to stay with?

Well, here's what happened for me, Stan. During that summer I had a couple of good buddies and we used to go around and look for work. But I must tell you this, I might have my time a little mixed up, yeah I think it's a little early for this. Well, anyway, in the first place you stay in a dormitory.
Well, that was what I was really getting at because that would add to the expense, wouldn't it?
All the way. And there's food.
I thought maybe you had an aunt or something like that.
No. Stayed on the campus.
Well, that was very good for you in a way.
Now as I see it, I think it's one of the finest things that ever happened to me. That's the way I feel about it.
JTHOMAS (1) 16
But it's still an expense to the family. Tremendous expense. Fortunately during that summer I don't want to leave Webster Grove, I met some and that little band -- may we go back to Webster Grove?
Sure. You take your own time.

We had quite a few people in that little town who were interested in what we were doing, older people, you know. And, some nights we'd split the band up and we'd go out, might be 5 or 6, and we'd play what you would call -- I don't know if you've ever seen a lawn party only for the kids and they'd pass the hat and sometimes you'd make 35¢. You dig with the lemonade, the sandwiches, the pretty girls, you know.
... Well you were playing dance music now.

Oh, no. We weren't professionals. I think the warmth of it is what it was because we weren't professionals but they were trying to give us some encouragement. I know the sound must have been terrible. It must/been.
Well, outdoors.

No, it must have been terrible but they did give us that encouragement and there were a lot of little girls there and there was a lot of lemonade and these jack-o-laterns strung places around the palees and listen to me, I've got to tell you this before beea I forget it. I was home during this year and a tremendous thing happened to me. A good buddy of mine stopped by.
JTHOMAS (1) 17
We called him B. Walker. He stopped by.
Called him what?

B. Walker. His name is William B. Walker. We called him B., you know. Well, my brother had arranged for a lot of the guys to stop by I hadn't seen in a long time but B. comes by the house and rings, knocks on the door and asks my brother, Rob says, "I want to talk, is Joe there?" He said, "Yeah, Joe's there." He said, "Well, there's a lady out there that wants to see him."
Just a second. So this guy says, "Is Joe there?"

Yeah. So this buddy of mine, B. Walker comes by. I'm at my brother's house which he remodeled. An old family house but he remodeled and did it up real prettily, you know. So he said, "Well, ask Joe to come to the door because there's a lady out here that wants to see him." Now, remember the jack-o-lanterns and also let me interject this idea, the player piano. You remember the player piano years ago?.
Yes.

So this lady here would invite us and she's friend of all of our families, invite us to her home and we'd have a chance to hear the player piano rolls and we'd have to pump. The only difference, the idea of pumping the piano, if you pump the piano that means you're not dancing so somebody's got your chick,man. You know what I mean? Now, right across
JTHOMAS (1) 18

the alleyway or right next door -- you know how it is in the country, you're not across the alleyway, you're right next door-- a man had a lot of influence, I mean, to me. He'd play all the blues records. That was my uncle, my Uncle Floyd. Uncle Floyd Thomas. I've got to mention him because a lot of things I heard that's the first time I heard them, you know.
Oh, this was where you would hear these blues records?

Yeah. Of course, now you know you can hear the blues, the blues is a tune. It's a tune, it's appeal a-feel, it's a lot of things, it's expression. And when it comes in the hands of people who can do it, that's a different interpretation and hasn't that hasn't changed as of today. I don't think so, do you?
No.
Well, (...) have all these records and ...
Well, I mean some people, everybody played the blues but some could put some feeling in them and make them mean something and others, it was nothing.
Well, thank you. That's what I was trying to say. That was exactly what I was trying to say.
Well, he'd have his records and these records would be Mamie Smith, Bessie Fletcher Smith, Sara Martin, Ma Rainey, you know.
Of course, when you hear those, now you're beginning to hear the people that played on those records, too, as well as the singers.
JTHOMAS (1) 19

Well, yes, I am. I think what I'm doing, too, yes I am, Stanley. I think what I'm doing, too, there might be -- yes, these are right in those years. You're quite right about too that and the thing that happened too -- you going to mention Helen?
(inaudible) Should we?

I don't see why we shouldn't, Stanley. You got it on, you got it off, huh? I don't see why we shouldn't. I think it might have happened during that time, Stan, because I'm beginning to get a chance to get acquainted with the cornet.
But, also I mean what I really meant was on records like Bessie Smith and Nomie Smith, etc., I mean they would be having these people like Joe Smith, Louis Armstrong, probably too.

Well, let me tell you about that. That's another part of the story. That's the reason I don't want to leave Webster Groves, you know. And, Joe Smith, beautiful trumpet player, you know, as you know .... And, Pops, always called Louis Armstrong, he was tremendous. And I think possibly the greatest horn (?) I've heard and a great guy. And ... I've got some funny stories to tell about Pops.
Well, we're going to come to that.
Now I've still got to get to Jeff City, huh?
What you're really talking about is what you'd heard before you left Webster Groves.
JTHOMAS (1)
Yes, but let me tell you about this.
You finish it up the player piano.

Yes. Well, the player piano -- this lady here, B. Walker comes by the house. There's a lady out here wants to see Joe. So I said, 'Well, fine.' Some pretty little chick stop by to see me, you know, even my wife can't resist that. You know I'm home but second time in 22 years. And had a most delicate and complete surprise I ever had in my life. This lady in our home we played -- she had two daughters -- Piano Rose (or piano rolls). Our families, they all knew each other. This lady was 91 years old. Her name was Mrs. Gleason Neesen, now her name is Mrs. Lipscomb (?) and she's still a jazz fan. And to bring me up to date, she said I know when you joined Fletcher Henderson. It was tremendous.

Now, see we had in Webster Groves, or outside Webster Groves they had things called roadhouses. I don't know if you know what a roadhouse is. Well, you might have an idea about it. A roadhouse in those days, Stan, at least the ones I played, there were fellows that had their families there, they might have had some other businesses but that was their love. That was their love, that was their instrument, you know. So, still haven't got to Jeff City, have we?
JTHOMAS (1) 21
No, but what you're trying to fill in here -- did you play in these roadhouses before you went to Jeff City?
Yes, before I went to Jeff City, oh, yeah.
You see in the summertime there were these lawn parties. some of you out of the band.

Well, no, this is a kid band now. See what I mean, Stan? This is a kid band. Yeah, before I went to Jeff City we had, a fellow stops by, two guys stopped by and they're old enough to be my father but they know our family. They come in, everybody know/s each other. So they need somebody to do something, make some noise to fill out the group and how in the world they ever thought about me, I'll never know. So my mother is out in the backyard washing the clothes. So they pass by me as I'm going out and they say, 'We want to talk to you about something.' So they ask my mother. I'll see what this is all about, you know. ... We want Joe to go to work with us. She said, 'Doing what?' He said, 'Playing the cornet.'
Want you to go play where, the roadhouse?
This roadhouse, you know.
Were they musicians?
Yeah, good musicians.
JTHOMAS (1) 22
But they were older guys?
Oh, yeah. Old men. I guess they must have been around -- as a kid thinks of an old man --
Who?

As a kid, you know. Anybody that's older, guy gets forty or something like that, you know. But, they were much older but they were tremendous persons. So, my mother she was a tremendous person. So she said, "No, I've got to wait until his dad comes home." And I really think she had her pictures in his mind, oh, the painted woman. Now think of me, here a kid (and niggers,) you know a-kid-and-a-nigger but take her, you know, and she is a beautiful person. Tremendous. And we went through a lot of things.
Well, I mean what went on at the roadhouses, drinking and dancing?

Listen, I haven't got there yet. Let me show what happened. So I got to wait, she's got to wait until dad gets home. So I'm saying, "Oh, Mom." You know I want to go. At least it's something different. And she said, "Well, I can't give you an answer until your dad comes home." So, that's a little hill and I can see my dad and my mother when they come over that hill because a lot of times before I want home to change my clothes, I'm out there shooting marbles. Say, "Joe, here comes your mom." It was too late, you know. So, this
JTHOMAS (1) 23

particular day I met my dad which I'd never done before. So he said, "Well, hi Joe." I say, "Hi, Pop." He said, "Well, what did you meet me for?" So I explained to him and he didn't say anything. He said, "Well, I got to talk to your mother." See my father and I could always get together I thought but this day is the day of decision and he's subject to go anywhere but I'm fussy. So they finally gave me their permission to go. Now, dig this. In Webster Groves when I come home at night, say we get off work at 1 o'clock and the guy who owns the joint wants to close, we get home at 12 o'clock. There's nobody on the streets. As the saying goes, the sidewalks are picked up. The only two things I could meet is an owl and a mule and I know both of them... Say, "hello owl," hello Joe, "hello mule," hello Joe.
WD: It was real
country.

Oh, yeah, I thought it was. But, permission I had to have. I couldn't have done this otherwise. So, the guys got tired of taking me home. They say, "Well, come on, Joe." They had to go somewhere to do some things, you know. "Do we have to take you home tonight?" I said, "no." And I was happy they didn't have to take me home. I got feet. I can walk by myself. A kid, around 12, 13 years old, something like that, I can walk home at night. The rest of the kids are asleep.
JTHOMAS (1)
So, it's a big deal.
Are you kidding? The moon is out there. It's tremendous.
Well, what sort of a band did they have at this roadhouse?
Well, we had three pieces. ... certainly we had piano, drums and a trumpet.
we almost had a three piece
Oh, I see. These two guys played piano and drums?
Yeah. You want their names?
Sure, if you remember them.
You do? Sure. Brown and Brad Bolden.
Bolden?
B-o-l-d-e-n. Brown played piano and Brad played the drums. Trap drums, as they used to call them in those days. And I'm sitting up there with my cornet.
Well, now what were you playing? You were playing sort of popular songs of the day, jazz or what?
Well, I think we were playing some pretty good things.
I mean where did you get to know them?

I got to know them through a sheet of ideas I had I guess, or maybe it just dropped on me. But, there's a tremendous trumpet player in St. Louis by the name of Charlie Creath and Big Babe of course, there was Dewey Jackson, Dick Babe (2).
JTHOMAS (1)
What was Big Babe's other name?
I don't know.
But where would you have heard them?
Well, I'm jumping the gun, Stan. I've heard them on the boats. But, now they were popular through that whole ...
Yeah but what I meant was when you started in that road house, presumably you were going to be sort of playing jazz of a kind, now you haven't had much experience of this before.
None.
But you had a good enough ear to make it with them?
Well, they thought so and I thought so, too.
And you learned quickly.
Well, I don't know. When you're 12 years old, had four years of lessons and I'd heard about Charlie Creath (?) and I'd listened to Louis Armstrong, whom I admired very much and I had a chance to ...
But, you'd heard him on records?

Records, yeah, up to that time. And, Mr. Langford, of course, was always an inspiration because of the things, not on popular tunes but he -- I'll tell you what he was.
